Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Vignette:
Raymond is a 69-year-old widowed financial analyst who presented for an initial assessment following what he described, with considerable understatement, as "a rough stretch." He is a man who has spent four decades reading markets, managing risk, and priding himself on composure under pressure. What brought him in was not a single breaking point but a slow accumulation of evidence that the strategies he had relied upon to stay functional were no longer holding.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Raymond's adult son, Daniel, was involved in a severe automobile accident. Raymond received the call at his desk — a Tuesday afternoon, numbers still open on his screen — and drove to the hospital alone. He arrived to find Daniel in surgery for internal bleeding, and he spent the next six hours in a waiting room, watching the clock, watching the door, saying nothing to anyone. Daniel survived, but the hours during which Raymond did not know whether his son would live constituted the core of what he now carries. He had watched a nurse approach the waiting room three separate times before she finally reached him, and each approach had felt like the arrival of the worst possible news. By the time Daniel was declared stable, something in Raymond had already been through the grief of losing him.

In the weeks that followed, Raymond noticed that certain moments would return to him without warning — the antiseptic smell of the corridor, the nurse's measured walk, the particular quality of silence in that room. These memories arrived unbidden and fully formed, interrupting a spreadsheet review or a phone call with a client. He did not speak of them to anyone. He had come to believe that examining them directly would only make them more real, and so he developed a habit of redirecting his attention the moment anything resembling that afternoon surfaced. He kept his schedule dense. He worked longer hours. He described his emotional life during this period as something he had "put in a drawer."

The difficulty was that the drawer kept opening. Conversations at work in which colleagues mentioned illness, bereavement, or the death of a parent would bring a wave of physical response — his chest tightening, his hands going cold, his heart rate climbing in a way that felt disproportionate and humiliating for a man his age and his professional standing. He began steering client conversations away from any mention of estate planning or inheritance, areas that his role as a financial analyst required him to address regularly. Over several months, two long-standing clients requested transfers to other advisors, citing a sense that Raymond had become "distant." He registered this as confirmation of something he already suspected about himself — that whatever he was managing internally was visible in ways he could not control.

Funerals became impossible. When a colleague's wife died in the autumn, Raymond sent flowers and did not attend the service. He told himself he had a conflict. He knew he did not. Cemeteries, grief announcements, memorial posts on professional networks — each one produced a visceral recoil that he managed by closing the browser, leaving the room, or, on one occasion, walking out of a restaurant when a nearby table began discussing a recent death in the family. What frightened him most was not the sadness itself but the anger that sometimes accompanied it — a sharp, sourceless irritability that had surfaced in a phone call with Daniel himself, of all people, leaving Raymond ashamed and confused about why he had raised his voice at the person whose survival had been the only thing he had wanted.

Raymond's wife had died seven years prior, and he had grieved her in what he considered an orderly way. He was not a man who thought of himself as someone who struggled. That self-understanding was precisely what had kept him from seeking help for over a year, and it was the growing gap between who he believed himself to be and how he was actually functioning that finally brought him to the office. He arrived composed, precise in his language, and visibly exhausted. What he said he wanted was to be able to do his job again. What he seemed to be asking, beneath that, was whether it was still possible to feel something without being undone by it.
